title: Teaching science is the context. Building metacognition is the goal.
subtitle: Pick a stage, a syllabus, and a real topic you'll actually teach. Then choose one of the nine teaching habits from the NSW metacognition guide. The tool shows you a specific classroom move — often a script you can say out loud — that builds students' awareness of their own thinking while they learn that science.
kicker: A worked example set for beginning science teachers
helperText: Nine habits from the NSW metacognition guide. Each is colour-coded by the phase of self-regulated thinking it mainly serves.
usageNote:
It's tempting to treat the Working Scientifically skills — questioning, planning, analysing — as “the metacognition”. They aren't. They're science skills: disciplinary content students learn, the same as photosynthesis or projectile motion. Metacognition is something more general — a student's awareness and regulation of their own thinking, which the research splits into metacognitive knowledge (knowing which strategies exist and when to use them) and regulation (planning, monitoring, evaluating your own cognition).

So the question this tool answers isn't “which syllabus skill is metacognitive?” It's the more useful one for a beginning teacher: while I'm teaching this particular bit of science, what can I actually do or say to make students more aware of how they're thinking? Every example keeps the science real and specific, then names the metacognitive move layered on top of it.

The nine habits come from the NSW Department of Education's Metacognition — a key to unlocking learning (2020). The specific classroom techniques draw on wider evidence: self-explanation and Predict–Observe–Explain, Claim–Evidence–Reasoning, confidence-rating and self-testing, exam wrappers, and social metacognition in group work.
attribution: The nine teaching habits and the three-phase (planning / monitoring / evaluating) framework are from NSW Department of Education, Metacognition — a key to unlocking learning (2020). The science topics and classroom moves are adapted for NSW secondary science curriculum-method study — an indication of changes made.
sources: NSW Department of Education (2020), Metacognition — a key to unlocking learning — the nine teaching habits and three-phase framework.
NSW Education Standards Authority — Science 7–10 Syllabus (2023) focus areas; Biology, Chemistry, Physics Stage 6 (2017) modules; and the 2025 Stage 6 syllabuses (implementation 2027–28).

Wider evidence base on metacognition in science: self-explanation & Predict–Observe–Explain (White & Frederiksen; Veenman et al.); Claim–Evidence–Reasoning argumentation; self-testing, spacing & interleaving and social metacognition (CBE–Life Sciences Education evidence-based teaching guide); confidence-accuracy calibration and exam wrappers.
